title: Students using AI to write essays

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Two thirds of the class admitted using it on the last essay. Anonymously, but two thirds.

turns.speaker: Ayo
turns.text: Used it how, though? Because there's a gap between asking it to explain a concept and asking it to write your conclusion.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: The survey didn't separate them, which I think was a mistake.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: It's the whole question. If a student argues with it for an hour and comes out understanding the material, that's a tutor. If they paste the question in, that's not.

turns.speaker: Ayo
turns.text: And the detectors don't work, before anyone suggests them. They flag non-native speakers at about twice the rate.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: Yes, and a false accusation is so much worse than a missed one that the tool is useless even at ninety per cent.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So what, we stop setting essays?

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: We stop setting essays that a machine can answer. Which, honestly, were never very good questions.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: Discuss the causes of the First World War is a prompt with a Wikipedia-shaped answer. It always was.

turns.speaker: Ayo
turns.text: Whereas something built on this term's seminar, or on data you collected yourself, is much harder to fake.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: That's more work to mark, though. Every one of those is different.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: It is. I'd rather mark thirty different essays than three hundred identical ones, mind you.

turns.speaker: Ayo
turns.text: Nobody's asked the students, either. Half of them would rather be examined in a way that meant something.

points: Two thirds of a class anonymously admitted using AI on their last essay, without distinguishing how.
Ayo and Marta argue the distinction matters: using it to understand material is tutoring, using it to produce the answer is not.
Detectors are rejected because they flag non-native speakers at roughly twice the rate, and a false accusation is far more damaging than a missed case.
Marta's proposal is to stop setting questions a machine can answer, arguing such prompts were always weak.
Better assessment ties work to a specific seminar or to data the student collected, which is harder to fake but more work to mark.
Ayo notes students have not been consulted and many would prefer assessment that meant something.
